title: Terrorism
hook: Terrorism is violence aimed less at its victims than at an audience — using fear as a political weapon to force change a group cannot win by other means.
key_points: Terrorism is the use of violence against civilians to advance a political aim through fear.
Its real target is an audience — the public or a government — not just those harmed.
It is often a tactic of the weak, used by groups lacking conventional power.
Defining it is contested: 'one group's terrorist' framing makes labels politically charged.
content_html: Terrorism is best understood not by the violence itself but by its logic. It is the use of violence — typically against civilians or non-combatants — to advance a political objective by spreading fear. The crucial feature is that the direct victims are usually not the real target. An attack is a message aimed at a wider audience: a population it seeks to frighten, a government it seeks to pressure or provoke, or a constituency it seeks to rally. The aim is to create a psychological and political effect out of proportion to the physical damage, which is why the same incident can dominate politics far beyond its immediate harm.
extra_html: Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that terrorism is frequently described as a "weapon of the weak": a tactic adopted by groups that lack the conventional military strength or political access to achieve their goals through ordinary means, and so seek leverage through fear instead. This also helps explain why governments respond to it as a security threat of a distinctive kind — one that targets a society's sense of safety and can push states toward measures that test the balance between security and civil liberties. A persistent difficulty is definition. Because calling an act "terrorism" is not neutral but condemnatory, the label is politically charged and fiercely contested — captured in the cliché that "one group's terrorist is another's freedom fighter," and complicated further by debates over whether states themselves can commit terrorism. Most working definitions therefore center on the core elements: violence, typically against civilians, intended to coerce or intimidate for a political purpose — while acknowledging that applying the term in practice is rarely free of politics.

related.title: War & Peace
related.hook: War is politics at its most extreme — organized violence between groups. Understanding why it happens, and how peace is kept, is central to the study of states.

related.title: Nuclear Weapons & Deterrence
related.hook: How do you stop a war you could never survive? The nuclear age answered with a chilling paradox: build weapons so terrible that no one dares use them.

related.title: Social Movements & Protest
related.hook: When ordinary channels fail or move too slowly, people organize and take to the streets. Social movements are how the unrepresented push change onto the agenda.

flashcards.prompt: What distinguishes terrorism from other violence?
flashcards.back_html: Its real target is an audience, not just the direct victims — it uses fear to advance a political aim.

flashcards.prompt: Why is terrorism often called 'a tactic of the weak'?

choices.text: It is typically used by groups lacking conventional military or political power
Because only powerful states ever use it

flashcards.explanation_html: Groups unable to win through conventional force or politics may turn to terror to exert influence disproportionate to their strength.

flashcards.prompt: Why is defining terrorism politically contested?

choices.text: Labeling an act 'terrorism' carries moral weight, so the term is fought over
Because no violence is ever political
Because everyone agrees on a single definition

flashcards.explanation_html: The label condemns, so groups and governments dispute who counts as a terrorist versus, say, a freedom fighter or a state actor.
